athens-georgia.intro: One oak in downtown Athens is said to own itself, along with the land within eight feet of its trunk. The tree standing on the corner of South Finley and Dearing today is the successor, raised from an acorn of the original and planted in 1946 after a windstorm took its parent. As far as Athens is concerned, the deed came with the acorn. There is a historical marker, a street corner, no fence and no fee, and a question of property law that nobody has ever bothered to settle in court.
athens-georgia.meta_description: An oak in downtown Athens is said to own itself. The Son of the Tree That Owns Itself was planted in 1946 from its parent's acorn.
athens-georgia.question_answer: The tree Athens is known for is the Son of the Tree That Owns Itself, a white oak of about eighty years standing on the corner of South Finley Street and Dearing Street, downtown. It is not the oldest tree in the city and it is the one worth the walk: it was planted on 4 December 1946, grown from an acorn of the original oak that fell in a windstorm in 1942. That original was, by a story the Athens Weekly Banner published in 1890, deeded ownership of itself and of the ground within eight feet of its trunk by Colonel William H. Jackson. Legal scholars doubt that a tree can hold property. Athens has never let the objection interfere. The plot is public, free and open at every hour, with a historical marker on the corner.
athens-georgia.question_meta: The Son of the Tree That Owns Itself stands at South Finley and Dearing in Athens, Georgia, planted in 1946 from the original's acorn.
athens-georgia.question_context: The corner of South Finley Street and Dearing Street sits on the western edge of downtown Athens, a few minutes on foot from the University of Georgia's North Campus and from Broad Street. There is nothing to book and no visitor centre. The plot is a corner of ground with a marker and a set of steps, and the tree on it is a white oak of ordinary size, because it is only eighty years old. The gap between the size of the tree and the size of the story is the visit. The original oak stood here for as long as anyone in Athens could remember and came down in a windstorm in 1942. The Junior Ladies Garden Club had thought ahead: they had an acorn from it, grew the seedling on, and planted it in the same plot on 4 December 1946, with horticulture students from the university doing the digging. Street parking is the usual approach. Nothing here is gated, ticketed or closed at night, which under the terms of the legend is only proper.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Athens, Georgia?
faq.a: The tree Athens is known for is not its oldest. The Son of the Tree That Owns Itself is a white oak of about eighty years, planted in 1946 from an acorn of the original that stood on the same corner and fell in 1942.

faq.q: Does the tree really own itself?
faq.a: By local tradition, yes. A story published in 1890 says Colonel William H. Jackson deeded the original tree ownership of itself and of the land within eight feet of its trunk. Legal scholars regard that as impossible under property law, and nobody has taken it to court to find out.

faq.q: Is it free to visit, and when is it open?
faq.a: Free, and open at any hour. It stands on a public street corner with a historical marker, no fence and no gate.

faq.q: How do I get there?
faq.a: It is on the corner of South Finley Street and Dearing Street, on the western edge of downtown Athens, a short walk from Broad Street and the University of Georgia's North Campus. Street parking nearby.

brunswick.intro: Albany Street splits in two just south of Prince Street and goes around a live oak. Brunswick built the road that way rather than move the tree, and local sources date Lover's Oak to the twelfth century, an age nobody has checked against a ring count. Ten heavy limbs branch low off a single trunk. A semi-truck took one of them off in 2015 and the tree carried on. It stands free and unfenced in the Old Town historic district, two blocks from the middle of downtown.
brunswick.meta_description: Brunswick built its street around this live oak. Lover's Oak stands in the middle of Albany Street, ten low limbs, dated by the town to the 1100s.
brunswick.question_answer: The oldest tree in Brunswick is Lover's Oak, a southern live oak standing in the middle of Albany Street just south of Prince Street, in the Old Town historic district. The city dates it to the twelfth century, roughly nine hundred years, with no ring count or growth rate behind the figure, so read it as the age Brunswick has always used rather than a measurement. Ten main limbs branch low off a trunk cited at thirteen feet through, low enough to see how they carry their own weight. The street was laid around the tree instead of through it, which is the reason most people stop. It is free, unfenced and reachable at any hour.
brunswick.question_meta: Lover's Oak, a live oak the town dates to the twelfth century, stands in the middle of Albany Street in Brunswick's Old Town district. Free.
brunswick.question_context: Brunswick's Old Town historic district is a grid of streets and squares laid out in the eighteenth century, and Albany Street runs through the middle of it. The oak sits in the roadway just south of Prince Street with traffic passing on both sides, so park on a side street and walk the last block rather than trying to stop beside it. There is no fence, no fee and no gate; this is public street furniture in the most literal sense the phrase allows. Ten main limbs branch low from the trunk, which is what gives the tree its shape and what makes it worth standing under rather than driving past. One of the ten came off in 2015 when a semi-truck hit it, and the wound is part of what you see. Southern live oaks hold their leaves through winter and exchange them in spring, so no month is the wrong one. What coastal Georgia does have is a hard summer, which is an argument for going early in the day rather than for going in another season.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Brunswick?
faq.a: Lover's Oak, a southern live oak in the middle of Albany Street just south of Prince Street. The city dates it to the twelfth century, about nine hundred years, though no ring count supports that figure.

faq.q: Is it free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. It stands in a public street in the Old Town historic district, unfenced, with no ticket and no opening hours.

faq.q: How do I get there, and where do I park?
faq.a: It is two blocks from central downtown Brunswick, at Albany and Prince. Park on a side street and walk the last block; the tree is in the roadway, with traffic passing on both sides.

faq.q: When is the best time to see it?
faq.a: Any month. Live oaks are evergreen and swap their leaves in spring without going bare, so there is no season to catch. Early morning is the kinder hour in a coastal Georgia summer.

chadds-ford.intro: The Battle of Brandywine was fought around this sycamore on 11 September 1777, when it was already 168 years old by the reckoning of the college that later raised a seedling from its seed. It stands beside the Gideon Gilpin farmhouse, where the wounded Marquis de Lafayette had his leg dressed that day. Five and a half metres round and thirty-four metres tall, with the flaking white upper limbs American sycamores show once the leaves are down. The battlefield grounds are free to walk and the tree is a short way in.
chadds-ford.meta_description: This sycamore was already 168 years old when the Battle of Brandywine was fought around it in 1777. It still stands by the Gilpin farmhouse.
chadds-ford.question_answer: The oldest tree in Chadds Ford is the Brandywine Sycamore, also called the Lafayette Sycamore, an American sycamore of roughly 400 years standing beside the Gideon Gilpin House in Brandywine Battlefield Park, off Baltimore Pike. Union County College, which grew a seedling from its seed in 1997, records the parent as dating from about 1609 and measuring 220 inches around and 111 feet tall, which made it 168 years old on the day of the battle in 1777. The farmhouse it stands beside is where the Marquis de Lafayette, shot through the leg, was taken to be treated. A 1987 bicentennial marker sits at its foot. The park grounds are free to walk; the house interior is seen on timed guided tours only.
chadds-ford.question_meta: The Brandywine Sycamore, about 400 years old, stands beside the Gideon Gilpin House at Brandywine Battlefield Park in Chadds Ford, PA.
chadds-ford.question_context: Brandywine Battlefield Park is off Baltimore Pike in Chadds Ford, roughly 40 km from central Philadelphia and about an hour by road. There is no public transport to it, so this is a car trip. The grounds are free to walk and the tree stands outside the Gideon Gilpin house, so seeing it costs nothing and takes minutes. The house interior is a different matter: timed guided tours only, Thursday to Sunday, so check the park's hours before you build a day around it. The battlefield is a National Historic Landmark covering the fighting of 11 September 1777, and the Gilpin farmhouse is where Lafayette was brought after a musket ball went through his leg. The sycamore beside it was, on Union County College's record, already 168 years old that afternoon. A bicentennial marker placed in 1987 stands at its base. The coordinates here mark the house rather than the trunk, because no tree-level fix has been published, but the two stand a yard apart, so nothing about that will cost you a search.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Chadds Ford?
faq.a: The Brandywine Sycamore, beside the Gideon Gilpin House at Brandywine Battlefield Park. It dates from about 1609 on the record of the college that propagated it, which makes it roughly 400 years old.

faq.q: Did this tree really witness the Battle of Brandywine?
faq.a: It was standing here and it was old enough. The battle was fought across these fields on 11 September 1777 and the tree was about 168 years old at the time, beside the farmhouse where Lafayette was treated. Nothing in the wood records the fighting; the claim rests on its age and its position, and both are documented.

faq.q: Is it free, and can I walk up to it?
faq.a: Yes. The park grounds are free and the tree stands in the open beside the house. Only the house interior is ticketed, on timed guided tours Thursday to Sunday.

faq.q: When is the best time to see it?
faq.a: January and February, when the leaves are down and the white upper limbs show, which is what a sycamore of this size does best. Summer gives you the shade and the 60-foot limb spread instead.

columbia.intro: A short drive southwest of Columbia, in the Missouri River bottoms near McBaine, one bur oak stands alone in a field: 7.3 metres around, a crown forty metres across, tied as national champion of its species. It was already about two hundred years old when Lewis and Clark came up the river in 1804, and it has taken lightning and the floods of 1993 and 1995 since. Bur Oak Road runs past it and the Katy Trail passes within yards, which is how most people arrive. Free, no gate, visible from the road.
columbia.meta_description: The Big Tree near Columbia was already 200 years old when Lewis and Clark passed. A champion bur oak, 7.3m round, free, right beside the Katy Trail.
columbia.question_answer: The oldest tree near Columbia is The Big Tree, officially the Williamson Bur Oak, standing on Bur Oak Road in the Missouri River bottoms near McBaine, a short drive southwest of the city. It is between 350 and 400 years old, sprouted some time in the 1600s, and measures 287 inches around, about 90 feet tall, with a crown 130 feet across, which has it tied as national champion bur oak and holding Missouri's state title since 1987. It has survived lightning strikes and the floods of 1993 and 1995, and an arborist keeps it under care; a May 2026 report described it as about as healthy as a nearly four-century-old tree can be. It stands on Williamson family land beside a public road, free to visit, with no gate.
columbia.question_meta: The Big Tree, a 350 to 400 year old champion bur oak, stands on Bur Oak Road near McBaine, a short drive from Columbia, Missouri. Free.
columbia.question_context: The Big Tree stands on Bur Oak Road in the Missouri River bottoms near McBaine, southwest of Columbia. There is no admission, no gate and no visitor centre: it is a tree in a field beside a public road, on land the Williamson family has farmed for six generations. The Katy Trail State Park rail-trail passes within yards, so a good share of the people who see it arrive by bicycle, and the flat gravel of the trail is the pleasant way to do it. Boone County made it an official historic site in August 2021, the only tree in the county with that designation, and it has been Missouri's state champion bur oak since 1987 as well as a tied national champion. What that means in front of you is a trunk 7.3 metres around and a crown forty metres wide with nothing else near it, which is why you pick it out from the road well before you arrive. The bottomland here is soft after heavy rain. Autumn is when the acorns drop, and a bur oak's are the size that stops people.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Columbia?
faq.a: The Big Tree, a bur oak of 350 to 400 years on Bur Oak Road near McBaine, a short drive southwest of the city. It is tied as national champion of its species and has been Missouri's state champion since 1987.

faq.q: Is it free, and is it on private land?
faq.a: Free, with no gate. The tree grows on the Williamson family's farmland, which they have held for six generations, but it stands right beside the public Bur Oak Road and people have been stopping for it for decades.

faq.q: Can I get there on the Katy Trail?
faq.a: Yes. The Katy Trail passes within yards of the tree, which is how many visitors arrive. By car it is a short drive southwest of Columbia to Bur Oak Road near McBaine.

faq.q: When is the best time to see it?
faq.a: September and October, when the big fringed acorns drop into the field. In winter the shape of a 40-metre crown with nothing beside it is easier to read, and after heavy rain the bottomland is soft underfoot.

coos-bay.intro: The tallest known Douglas fir on Earth stood in the hills of Coos County until August 2025, when a fire nobody has explained burned for days in its crown. The Doerner Fir survived it, about fifteen metres shorter and no longer the record holder. It is roughly 450 years old and still among the tallest trees anywhere that are not redwoods. The trail in is short and marked; the road in is an hour of BLM forest road, the last stretch gravel and unmaintained in winter. Free, on public land.
coos-bay.meta_description: A fire took 15 metres off the Doerner Fir in August 2025 and it lived. The former tallest Douglas fir on Earth, on BLM land in Coos County.
coos-bay.question_answer: The oldest and tallest tree in Coos County is the Doerner Fir, a Douglas fir of roughly 450 years on BLM land off Upper East Fork Brummit Road, reached by a signed trailhead about an hour's drive from Roseburg. Until August 2025 it was the tallest known Douglas fir on Earth at 325.8 feet, or 99.3 metres. That month a fire of unexplained origin burned for several days in its crown; firefighters put it out and the tree lived, but it lost around fifty feet off the top and the record with it. No official remeasurement has been published since, so the height given here, about 84 metres, is an approximation from press coverage rather than a survey. Access is free, on public land, by a short marked trail.
coos-bay.question_meta: The Doerner Fir, about 450 years old, is the former tallest Douglas fir on Earth. On BLM land in Coos County, free, by a short marked trail.
coos-bay.question_context: The Doerner Fir stands on BLM land in the Coast Range of eastern Coos County, off Upper East Fork Brummit Road. There is no public transport and no shortcut. The usual approach is about an hour's drive from Roseburg, mostly on paved BLM forest road with the last four and a half miles on gravel, and that road is not maintained through the winter, so check conditions before setting out. The trailhead has its own parking area and a register to sign, and from there a short marked trail drops to the tree. All of it is free and open. What waits at the bottom changed in August 2025, when a fire burned for several days in the crown and firefighters worked it until it was out. The tree came through. It lost roughly fifty feet off the top and with it the title of tallest known Douglas fir on Earth, previously measured at 325.8 feet, among the tallest non-redwood trees recorded anywhere. It was known as the Brummit Fir before it was renamed for a Douglas County commissioner.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Coos Bay?
faq.a: The Doerner Fir, a Douglas fir of roughly 450 years standing on BLM land in eastern Coos County. It was the tallest known Douglas fir on Earth until a fire cost it about fifteen metres of crown in August 2025.

faq.q: Is the Doerner Fir still alive after the 2025 fire?
faq.a: Yes. The fire burned for several days in the crown, firefighters extinguished it, and the tree survived with its top gone. It is no longer the record holder and it is still standing.

faq.q: How do I get there, and is it free?
faq.a: Free, on public land, with no permit. Drive about an hour from Roseburg on BLM forest roads, the last four and a half miles gravel, to a signed trailhead with parking. The road is not maintained in winter.

faq.q: How tall is it now?
faq.a: Around 84 metres by press estimates after the fire, down from a measured 325.8 feet, or 99.3 metres. Nobody has published an official remeasurement, so treat the current figure as approximate.

chapel-hill.intro: The oldest quad at the University of North Carolina has a tulip tree at the middle of it, and campus legend holds that the university sits where it does because General William R. Davie fell asleep under that tree in 1792. The Davie Poplar is over 100 feet tall, over 16 feet round, and 300 to 375 years old on the university's own estimate, which puts it here before the university whichever end of the range you take. Two propagated descendants grow beside it. McCorkle Place is open ground, free, and busy all day.
chapel-hill.meta_description: Campus legend says UNC stands where it does because a man napped under this tulip tree in 1792. The Davie Poplar, 300 to 375 years old.
chapel-hill.question_answer: The oldest tree in Chapel Hill is the Davie Poplar, a tulip tree of 300 to 375 years standing on McCorkle Place, the oldest quad of the University of North Carolina, a two-minute walk from Franklin Street. It is more than 100 feet tall and more than 16 feet around, and the university's age estimate has no ring count behind it, so take the band rather than a single figure. Even at the low end it predates the university. Campus legend says General William R. Davie napped beneath it in 1792 and chose the site for the university on the strength of it, which is a story rather than a record. Two younger propagations, Davie Poplar Jr. and Davie Poplar III, grow nearby and are often mistaken for it. The quad is free and open.
chapel-hill.question_meta: The Davie Poplar, a tulip tree of 300 to 375 years, stands on McCorkle Place at UNC in Chapel Hill. Open ground, free, minutes from Franklin Street.
chapel-hill.question_context: McCorkle Place is the northern quad of the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, bounded by Franklin Street at one end, so the tree is a two-minute walk from the middle of town. It is open ground crossed by paths, free and unfenced, busy from morning to evening, and nobody stops anyone walking in. The poplar stands near the centre with the Old Well and Old East close by, which makes this a short walk with a lot on it. Davie Poplar Jr., rooted from the original, and Davie Poplar III, propagated later, grow nearby and get mistaken for the parent regularly, so look for the largest of the three. The university estimates the age at 300 to 375 years without a ring count behind it, which is honest of them and worth repeating rather than rounding. Seeds from the tree were handed out to students in 2005, and the campus paper was still writing about that giveaway twenty years later. Autumn is the moment: tulip trees turn a clear yellow, usually in the second half of October here.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Chapel Hill?
faq.a: The Davie Poplar, a tulip tree on McCorkle Place at UNC, estimated at 300 to 375 years by the university. No ring count supports the figure, so it is a broad estimate rather than a measurement.

faq.q: Which one is the original?
faq.a: The largest of the three. Davie Poplar Jr. was rooted from the original and Davie Poplar III was propagated later; both stand nearby and both get photographed by mistake.

faq.q: Can I walk onto the quad, and does it cost anything?
faq.a: Yes and no. McCorkle Place is open campus green with paths across it, free, unfenced, and used all day by students and everyone else.

faq.q: When does it look its best?
faq.a: Late October, when the crown turns clear yellow. Tulip trees also flower in May and June, green and orange, but the flowers sit high in the crown and are easy to miss from below.

fish-lake.intro: Pando is a single quaking aspen with roughly 40,000 trunks. One root system, about 106 acres, every stem genetically identical, and by mass it is commonly reckoned the largest living thing on Earth. Its age is a genuine argument rather than a rounded number, running from several hundred years to 80,000 depending on the method used. A flat 1.4 mile trail from the Old Spanish Trailhead by Fish Lake walks straight into it. There is no single trunk to photograph, which is exactly what makes the walk worth taking.
fish-lake.meta_description: Pando is one aspen with 40,000 trunks and one root system, spread over 106 acres by Fish Lake, Utah. A flat trail walks straight into it.
fish-lake.question_answer: The oldest living thing at Fish Lake is Pando, a single quaking aspen made up of roughly 40,000 stems sharing one root system across about 106 acres, entered from the Old Spanish Trailhead on Highway 25 in Fishlake National Forest. Its age is disputed and we are not going to narrow it: the popular figure of 80,000 years comes from an assumed rate of spread, and other researchers argue for anything from several hundred years to about 14,000. What is not disputed is the mass, which is why Pando is commonly described as the largest known living organism on Earth. A flat 1.4 mile out and back from the trailhead runs a spur directly through the clone. Free, no permit, US Forest Service land.
fish-lake.question_meta: Pando, one quaking aspen of 40,000 stems on one root system, spreads over 106 acres at Fish Lake, Utah. Free, no permit, flat 1.4 mile trail.
fish-lake.question_context: Pando lies beside Highway 25, the Fishlake Scenic Byway, on the southwest side of Fish Lake in Fishlake National Forest, central Utah. The nearest town is Richfield, about 25 minutes away; there is no public transport, and the byway can close with snow. Parking is at the Old Spanish Trailhead, which is signed, free and needs no permit. From there a flat 1.4 mile walk out and back on the Lakeshore National Recreation Trail runs a spur directly through the clone, and an overlook reachable off Forest Road 046N shows the extent of it from outside. The Forest Service manages the site, and researchers are actively studying whether the clone can still replace itself, because deer and cattle browse the young stems before they clear head height. Nothing here is closed to visitors. The one thing to understand before arriving: there is no single trunk and no viewpoint that holds the whole organism, so you walk into it rather than up to it, and the stems on either side of the path are all one thing.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Fish Lake?
faq.a: Pando, and it is not really a tree in the usual sense: it is one quaking aspen expressed as about 40,000 stems on a shared root system. Age estimates run from several hundred years to 80,000 and researchers do not agree on a method, so no single figure is settled.

faq.q: Is Pando one tree or a forest?
faq.a: One organism. Every stem is genetically identical and connected underground, which is why the whole hillside changes colour in the same week each autumn. It looks like a forest and behaves like a single plant.

faq.q: How do I get there, and is it free?
faq.a: Free, no permit. Park at the Old Spanish Trailhead on Highway 25 by Fish Lake, about 25 minutes from Richfield, Utah, and walk the flat 1.4 mile trail that runs into the clone. The scenic byway can close with snow.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit?
faq.a: Late September into early October, when every stem turns gold in the same week. That synchrony is the visible proof that it is all one organism.

guerneville.intro: Two of the oldest coast redwoods in Sonoma County stand within five minutes of each other at Armstrong Redwoods, on flat ground a short walk from the car park. Colonel Armstrong is around 1,400 years old and 300 feet tall, named for the lumberman who set this stand aside instead of cutting it. The Parson Jones Tree is the taller of the two at over 310 feet and stands a hundred yards from the entrance. Both came through the Walbridge Fire in 2020. Day use fee, easy trail, evergreen all year.
guerneville.meta_description: Two ancient coast redwoods at Armstrong Redwoods near Guerneville: Colonel Armstrong at about 1,400 years, and the taller Parson Jones Tree.
guerneville.question_answer: The oldest tree in Guerneville is Colonel Armstrong, a coast redwood of roughly 1,400 years standing about half a mile up the main trail in Armstrong Redwoods State Natural Reserve, on Armstrong Woods Road just north of town. Estimates for it run from about 1,200 to 1,600 years, and it reaches around 300 feet. It is named for Colonel James B. Armstrong, the lumberman who set this old-growth stand aside from logging in the 1870s and 1880s. The Parson Jones Tree, roughly 1,300 years old and over 310 feet, is the tallest in the grove and stands about a hundred yards from the parking area, so the two make one flat walk of well under an hour. State Parks charges a day use fee of about ten dollars per vehicle.
guerneville.question_meta: Colonel Armstrong, a coast redwood of about 1,400 years, stands in Armstrong Redwoods near Guerneville, with the taller Parson Jones Tree nearby.
guerneville.question_context: Armstrong Redwoods State Natural Reserve is on Armstrong Woods Road, about five minutes' drive north of Guerneville in the Russian River valley. There is no public transport. California State Parks charges a day use fee of roughly ten dollars per vehicle, and walking in is possible when the lot fills. Both named trees sit on the main loop and the ground is flat: the Parson Jones Tree is about a hundred yards from the parking area, Colonel Armstrong about half a mile in, so seeing the pair takes well under an hour at a slow pace. Other named giants, the Icicle Tree and Burbank Circle among them, stand on the same loop. This is old growth that was never logged, because Armstrong, who made his money cutting Sonoma County forest, kept this stand out of it. In August 2020 the Walbridge Fire reached the reserve and crews worked to protect the grove; it burned at the edges and the big trees came through. Redwoods are evergreen, so any month works, and the grove holds cool air on a hot day.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Guerneville?
faq.a: Colonel Armstrong, a coast redwood of roughly 1,400 years in Armstrong Redwoods State Natural Reserve, about half a mile along the flat main trail from the entrance. Estimates for it range from about 1,200 to 1,600 years.

faq.q: Is there an entrance fee?
faq.a: Yes. California State Parks charges a day use fee of about ten dollars per vehicle at Armstrong Redwoods. Walking in on foot is possible, which people do when the parking area fills.

faq.q: How far is the walk, and is it accessible?
faq.a: Short and flat. The Parson Jones Tree is roughly a hundred yards from the parking area and Colonel Armstrong about half a mile further on the main loop, so both together is well under an hour at a slow pace.

faq.q: Did the 2020 fires destroy the grove?
faq.a: No. The Walbridge Fire reached the reserve in August 2020 and crews worked to hold it. The edges burned and the old trees survived, helped by redwood bark that runs a foot thick and carries little resin.

hampton.intro: The Emancipation Proclamation was read to the South for the first time under this live oak, in September 1863, to the free and newly freed Black community of the Virginia Peninsula. Mary Peake had already taught children to read beneath it, at a time when Virginia law forbade teaching them. The tree still stands on the Hampton University campus, canopy about 98 feet across, and is still used for ceremonies. Its age is unsettled, with estimates from 200 to over 300 years. Open campus ground, free, nothing between you and it.
hampton.meta_description: The Emancipation Proclamation was first read in the South under this live oak in 1863. It still stands on the Hampton University campus, free to visit.
hampton.question_answer: The oldest tree in Hampton is the Emancipation Oak, a southern live oak on the Hampton University campus near the corner of East Queen Street and Tyler Street, estimated at somewhere between 200 and 300 years. The estimates disagree badly: older material says 150 to 200 years, a 2023 figure says about 250, a 2022 report says 309, and nobody has cored the tree to settle it, deliberately, because taking a core from an old live oak for the sake of a number is a poor trade. In September 1863 the Black community of the Virginia Peninsula gathered beneath it for the first public reading of the Emancipation Proclamation in the South. Its canopy spreads about 98 feet on a trunk about 50 feet tall. The campus grounds are open and free.
hampton.question_meta: The Emancipation Oak, roughly 200 to 300 years old, stands on the Hampton University campus where the Emancipation Proclamation was read in 1863.
hampton.question_context: The Emancipation Oak stands on the Hampton University campus near the corner of East Queen Street and Tyler Street, on open ground with no fence, no ticket and no restriction on walking up to it. The campus is a National Historic Landmark district, listed on the National Register in November 1969, and this tree is part of what earned it that. Hampton sits on the Virginia Peninsula and the campus is straightforward to reach by car from I-64, with parking nearby. Mary Peake taught free and enslaved Black children to read beneath these branches when Virginia law forbade it. In September 1863 the community gathered here for the first Southern public reading of the Emancipation Proclamation, and the university still holds ceremonies under the tree. What you see is a southern live oak doing what live oaks do with space, spreading a canopy about 98 feet across on a trunk barely 50 feet tall. It is evergreen, so no season is better than another. National Geographic once listed it among ten great trees of the world.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Hampton?
faq.a: The Emancipation Oak on the Hampton University campus, a southern live oak estimated at 200 to 300 years. Published figures range from 150 to 309 years and nobody has cored it, so the number is genuinely open.

faq.q: Why is it called the Emancipation Oak?
faq.a: Because the Emancipation Proclamation was read publicly under it in September 1863, the first such reading in the South, to the Black community of the Virginia Peninsula. Mary Peake had taught freed and enslaved children to read there before that.

faq.q: Can I visit it, and does it cost anything?
faq.a: Yes, and no. It stands on open campus ground within Hampton University's National Historic Landmark district, free, unfenced, with nothing between you and the tree.

faq.q: When is the best time to see it?
faq.a: Any time. Southern live oaks are evergreen and hold their leaves through winter, so the tree looks much the same all year. The university's own Emancipation Day gatherings are held beneath it.

lebec.intro: A trapper named Peter Lebeck was killed by a grizzly bear here in October 1837 and buried under a valley oak, with the date cut into its bark. The tree grew over the lettering and sealed it in; when the bark was cut away decades later, the inscription was found mirrored on the underside, pressed there as the wound healed. The oak stands at Fort Tejon State Historic Park in Grapevine Canyon beside I-5, with a 1938 headstone copying the words. Open daily, day use vehicle fee.
